newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan soldier gets life for killing Israeli girls.
newsitem.headline: Jordan soldier gets life for killing Israeli girls.

text.p: A military court in Jordan on Saturday sentenced a soldier to life imprisonment with hard labour for shooting dead seven Israeli schoolgirls on a patch of borderland in March.
The five-man panel of military judges said army private Ahmed Daqamsa was guilty of murder but ruled out premeditation, which could have brought a death sentence.

Daqamsa's attack four months ago outraged King Hussein, who travelled to Israel to pay condolences to the families of the Israeli girls. But opponents of Jordan's three-year peace with Israel rallied to defend the soldier.

"In the light of his psychological state it was not at all possible for the defendant to have had composure, balance, deliberation and ability of prior planning and self-control, which means premeditation was not existent," tribunal head Brigadier Mamoun Khasawneh said.
Daqamsa, reading occasionally from the Moslem holy book, the Koran, was unusually cheerful as he sat during the hearing behind the black bars of his cage in the dock.
He was calm when his sentence, the maximum punishment for murder without premeditation, was read out. Daqamsa has no right to appeal, lawyers said.

His wife Fatima, barred from the court on Saturday, screamed with grief when told by reporters of the sentencing. Family members chanted anti-government slogans outside the military base while riot police with batons stood by.
Jordan's Minister of State for Information Samir Mutawae said Daqamsa had received a fair trial and Israel's government spokesman said the verdict was "eminently justified".
But Margalit Bedayev, mother of one of the dead schoolgirls, said: "For murdering seven girls he should have received the death sentence."
Jordanian opponents of the peace deal with Israel said Daqamsa was being sacrificed so that Jordan's close ties with Israel would not be harmed.
"It was a political trial right from the beginning," said member of parliament Toujan Feisal. "Any soldier would have acted in the same way...He was a soldier who was acting against occupiers."
In a unanimous ruling, the judges said Daqamsa knew what he was doing when he shot the girls, but said his mental disorder made him act impulsively without regard for consequences.

The tribunal also found Daqamsa guilty on three charges of intent to kill, threatening to kill and military disobedience, for which he was sentenced to a total of 14 years, to run concurrently with the life sentence.
It also dismissed defence claims about the unconstitutional nature of the trial and claims that Israeli investigators were illegally involved.
Daqamsa opened fire on the schoolgirls while they were visiting the border territory of Baqoura, returned to Jordan under a 1994 peace accord but then leased back to Israel.
Khasawneh said Daqamsa's mentally troubled state was exacerbated on the day of the shooting by the pressure of intense exhaustion. He had been on duty for 22 hours non-stop.
He added that Daqamsa also had an obsession with sex, which took hold of him when he saw the girls.
"He was in a sexually aroused state after seeing the girls and with 22 hours on duty, this worsened his personality disorder and made him unable to control himself," he said.
Daqamsa fired nearly three clips of ammunition at the girls until his gun jammed and he was overpowered by comrades.

The defence had pleaded for the acquittal of their client on grounds his anti-social personality disorder was a psychological illness which made him unaccountable for his actions as a result of diminished responsibility.
